title: Partner CBT — Light
description: Having a partner apply manual pressure to the cock and balls introduces a dynamic element the solo version doesn't have: someone else calibrating and controlling an area the receiver is particularly attuned to. That's often as activating as the physical sensation itself.
safetyNote: Build pressure very gradually — start lighter than feels necessary and increase only on clear positive feedback. Agree on a clear word to stop before starting.

instructions.label: With a partner
instructions.content: Receiver lies back with the area accessible. Giver begins with very light contact: cupping, gentle rolling of the testicles, a light grip along the shaft — well below what the solo version has established the receiver can handle. Build slowly. Try sustained compression held at different levels. Try slow traction — steady downward pulling of the scrotum, released and repeated. Try light squeezing along the shaft. The receiver's job is to notice what receiving this from a partner produces differently from the solo version — whether the dynamic element changes how the same sensations land. The giver's job is to read feedback closely and stay in complete control throughout. After one round, switch.

explore: As receiver: does receiving this from a partner produce anything beyond what the solo version produces — and what accounts for the difference?
Is the dynamic element — someone else in control of this specific area — part of what makes it interesting, or primarily the physical sensation?
As giver: does the particular responsibility of controlling this area — where the consequences of misjudgement are specific — produce a different quality of attention from other touch?
Is there a clear role preference, and does it align with your preferences elsewhere in the guide?
why: The partner version of light CBT differs from the solo version for the same reason most partner experiences differ: fuller relaxation is possible, and the dynamic element is real. Here the dynamic element is more concentrated than usual — the giver has control of an area the receiver is particularly attuned to, and both people know it. That power dynamic operates in parallel with the physical sensation, and for many people it does at least as much of the work. What the solo exploration established about range and preference now becomes a shared language: the receiver knows what they respond to, and the giver has precise information to work with.
